titleStmt.title: Letter from John Chamberlain to Dudley Carleton, 1 March 1599

publicationStmt.p: Published digitally at earlymodernletters.org. Licensed under CC BY 4.0.

div.p: I receved both your letters of the 12th and twentieth of the last, full fraught both with theyre owne store, and much other goode matter that came in theyre companie. We kepe still at a stay and do neither movere nor promovere,"We neither move nor make headway" — a Latin phrase from Terence expressing inertia. Chamberlain applies it to the general stalemate in English affairs: the Irish expedition neither advancing to departure nor officially called off. but drive on with the weather to see what time will bringe foorth.

The erle of Essex is crased, "Crased" = mentally or physically unsettled; broken in health or spirit. By early March 1599 Essex had suffered weeks of humiliating reversals over his Irish commission — quarrels about the title, the powers, the officers, the finances — and was reportedly making it a question whether he would go at all. but new difficulties arise dayly about his commission, as touching the time and touching the disposing of his abode, touching his intertainment,The "entertainment" of an Elizabethan commander meant the pay and allowances attached to his office. Essex was dissatisfied with the financial terms offered for the Irish command, as well as with the arrangements for who would control places and offices in his absence from court. and the disposing of places and offices, upon which points and some others he is so litle satisfied that many times he makes yt a question whether he go or not. Sir George Carie of CockingtonSir George Carey of Cockington, Devon (not to be confused with George Carey, second Baron Hunsdon and Lord Chamberlain of England). He was a West Country gentleman associated with the Plymouth region, now named to the important administrative post of Treasurer of Ireland — responsible for managing the crown's financial operations in the colony. (by Plymouth) is named to be treasurer of Ireland in Sir Henry WallopsSir Henry Wallop (c. 1531–1599), Treasurer at Wars of Ireland from 1579 until his death in 1599. His long tenure had given him an unrivalled knowledge of the Irish financial system; Chamberlain's aside — "whether he be to my Lords liking or no I know not" — implies that Essex had not been consulted about Carey's appointment, and was not pleased. place, but whether he be to my Lords liking or no I know not.

The rebells of Mounster and Connagh are not so united but that they have many jarres among themselves, and of late a bickering, wherin Patricke CondonPatrick Condon, a Munster Gaelic lord and prominent rebel leader in the Nine Years' War. His reported death or serious wounding here illustrates the factional tensions among the Ulster-Munster rebel alliance that the English had been trying to exploit. (a cheife ringleader) is saide to be slaine or sore hurt.

Here was newes that Captaine Simmes and his companie was cut apeeces by the ennemie, but as far as I heare since, yt was but a private quarrell in which Sims miscaried.A reminder that military news from Ireland — even alarming news of a company destroyed — was routinely garbled in transmission. What reached London as an enemy action turned out to be an internal brawl. On Satterday last Sir William Woodhouse accompanied with fowre hacksters,Hired swords; men paid to do violence. "Hackster" (also "huckster" or "hackster") was the period term for a hired ruffian, distinct from a gentleman duelling on point of honour. understanding that Sir Robert DrurySir Robert Drury (c. 1575–1615) of Hawsted, Suffolk, courtier and soldier. The motive for Woodhouse's attack is not stated, but Woodhouse had been at the centre of the Essex–Nottingham quarrel over a Low Countries regiment in January 1599 (see Letter 15), and Drury may have been connected to that dispute. Drury later achieved distinction as a patron of John Donne, who would write his famous elegy on the death of Drury's daughter Elizabeth — the "First Anniversary." was to come from Totnam toward London, waited for him in the way, and set upon him as he was comming out of his coach, wounding him in three or fowre places, and thincking they had dispatched him, left him for dead, but yt falles out better with him, for he is like to recover; mary his man that offred himself in his masters defence was slaine outright in the place. Upon the first alarme at the court, there was commaundment from the counsaile for a privie search all over this towne to apprehend them, but within two howres after (upon what reason I know not) yt was countermaunded.The countermanding of the privy search within two hours — with no explanation offered — would have been a conspicuous detail to Chamberlain and his readers. It suggests either that Woodhouse's connection to Essex bought him protection, or that the government did not want to embarrass powerful patrons by pursuing the matter too publicly. Some geve out that Sir William Woodhouse shold be likewise hurt in the face and in the hande, but I thincke yt is rather geven out to move pitie then otherwise, for I cannot learne he was neere daunger, and the match was very uneven of five to two, and they taken on the sodain.

The Lady Drury (Sir Roberts mother) died some ten or twelve dayes since and hath left Sir John Scot a fresh widower.Lady Drury was Elizabeth, daughter of Sir William Stafford of Grafton, who had first married Sir William Drury of Hawsted (Sir Robert's father) and then Sir John Scott of Nettlestead, Kent. Her death makes her second husband a widower again — hence Chamberlain's "fresh widower." The coincidence of her death so close to her son's ambush gave the passage an additional air of calamity in the Drury household. I wrote you in one of my letters that Sir W. Woodhouse had married the Lady Southwell, but the matter was mistaken, though yt were generally bruited.

One Doctor LedsamIdentified by McClure as presumably Henry Ledsham, a clergyman who had served as one of the Queen's chaplains but was apparently long regarded as mentally unstable. Suicide was an act of profound theological transgression in early modern England — self-murder — and Chamberlain's phrase "made away himself" was the standard euphemism for it. sometimes the Quenes chaplain, but allwayes a giddibraind fellow, hath lately stab'd and made away himself here in towne. The match is made up twixt younge NorrisFrancis Norris (c. 1579–1622), son of the first Baron Norris of Rycote; he succeeded as second Baron Norris of Rycote and was later created first Earl of Berkshire (1621). His match with Bridget Vere united two prominent Protestant noble families. and the Lady BrigetBridget Vere (c. 1584–1631), second daughter of Edward de Vere, seventeenth Earl of Oxford. Her father was the poet and courtier long identified in some traditions with the authorship controversy surrounding Shakespeare; whatever the truth of that identification, he was one of the most culturally prominent noblemen of the Elizabethan court. Bridget and Francis Norris were married in 1599. second daughter to the erle of Oxford.Edward de Vere (1550–1604), seventeenth Earl of Oxford; Lord Great Chamberlain of England; poet and patron of players. His daughters were considered advantageous matches for Protestant gentlemen seeking connections to the older nobility.

We are still fed with fresh rumors of Don SebastianDon Sebastião I of Portugal (1554–1578), who died at the Battle of Alcácer Quibir in Morocco. His body was never conclusively identified, and "Sebastianism" — the messianic belief that he would return — persisted in Portugal for generations. Periodically, impostors claiming to be Sebastian appeared in Europe; this is one such rumour. Chamberlain's sceptical "I will lay no wager of all this" is characteristic. that he is ipsissimus,"The very man himself" — a Latinate way of saying the claimant is the real Sebastian rather than an impostor. and that the Venetians have sent ambassadors to the king of Spaine to signifie so much unto him: and that there have ben some great men executed of late in Portingale about this busines, and many others translated into Spaine, but I will lay no wager of all this.

For lacke of better matter I send you three or fowre toyes to passe away the time: the letter of SquiresEdward Squire (d. 1598), the alleged poisoner of the Queen and Essex — see Letters 9 and 10. The pamphlet Chamberlain sends, A Letter written out of England to an English Gentleman at Padua (1599, attributed to Francis Bacon), gave a polished official account of the conspiracy and Squire's confession and execution. conspiracie is well written, but the other of Dr. DeeJohn Dee (1527–1608 or 1609), mathematician, astrologer, and self-described conjuror of spirits, who had fallen out of royal favour and spent his last decades in poverty and controversy. The pamphlet Chamberlain refers to is probably Dee's A Letter containing a most brief discourse apologeticall (1599), in which Dee defended himself against charges of conjuring and imposture. Chamberlain's "ridiculous bable of an old imposturinge jugler" is one of his sharpest dismissals. is a ridiculous bable of an old imposturinge jugler. The Silkeworme is thought to be Dr. MuffetsThomas Moffet (or Moffett, 1553–1604), physician and naturalist, author of The Silkworms and Their Flies (1599), a didactic poem on sericulture. Chamberlain's attribution was correct. and in mine opinion is no bad peece of Poetrie. The treatise of Henry the fourth is reasonablie well written. The author is a younge man of Cambridge;This is John Hayward's The First Part of the Life and Raigne of King Henrie the IIII (1599), dedicated to the Earl of Essex. The book's account of the deposition of Richard II was read as dangerous political allegory — implying Essex might do to Elizabeth what Bolingbroke did to Richard. Elizabeth herself reportedly said: "I am Richard II, know ye not that?" and many exceptions were taken toward yt, why there was a short thinge in Latin dedicated to the erle of Essex,The printed dedication to Essex was the chief offence: it appeared to identify Essex as a new Bolingbroke, capable of deposing the reigning monarch. The Privy Council ordered the dedication cut from the book. Hayward was later summoned before the Star Chamber and imprisoned in the Tower. and objected to him in goode earnest, wherupon there was commaundment yt shold be cut out of the booke, yet I have got you a transcript of yt that you may picke out the offence yf you can; for my part I can finde no such buggeswords,"Buggeswords" — McClure glosses this as "terrifying words." The term (from "bugge" or "bogey," a frightening apparition) means language designed to scare rather than to make a genuine seditious argument. Chamberlain cannot see what the fuss is about — which may say something about his politics or simply about the opacity of the offending passage to a casual reader. but that every thinge is as yt is taken.

I am going the next weeke (God willing) to Knebworth, in which consideration I am not greatly sory for your stayeng at Ostend, for I shold have injoyed but litle of your company, which perhaps there will come better to passe both here and at some other time. And so wishing you all contentment I commit you to God.

closer.dateline: From London this first of March 1599.

postscript.p: To my very goode frend Master Dudley Carleton attending on the Lord Governor of Ostend geve these.
